paras: The beating of Lieutenant Marion R. Perry took place at Peffler's department store in Little Rock, Arkansas, on or shortly before June 20, 1919, when store clerks attacked the army officer after he protested being refused a money order. Perry was left bleeding from several wounds, and the clerk who struck first was arrested. Black newspapers presented the case as an insult to a returned soldier, and one counted it among the outrages of that year.
Perry was a lieutenant in the 317th ammunition train of the 92nd division. Formerly of Pine Bluff, he had come to Little Rock to take charge of the uniform ranks of the Mosaic Temple of America.

Perry tried to buy a money order at the post-office substation inside Peffler's store, at 6th and Main streets, and was refused service. When he demanded an explanation and did not heed the clerk's "Move away quickly" order, the clerk, whose name was "said to be" Swatzheimer, came from behind the cage and struck him in the left eye. Before Perry could regain his feet, all the clerks in the store set upon him, and a shoe rack in one clerk's hands cut a deep gash in his head. He was taken from the store bleeding from several wounds.

A few hours after the fight, Swatzheimer was placed under arrest. Black residents were advised to stop buying goods at Peffler's "until the matter has been properly adjusted," and Perry placed his case with two prominent local attorneys. No report of a charge, trial or settlement appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Defender ran the Little Rock dispatch on its front page of June 21 under the headline "Soldier Who Resented Insult Is Beaten," spelling the clerk's name "Swathelmier" and the store "Peffers." The dispatch opened by saying the officer had fought "his greatest battle, not on French soil," but in a Little Rock store. The Colorado Statesman reprinted the same text on its front page of July 5.

A week earlier, the Statesman's editorial "The Darkest Hour" had already listed "the terrible beating and maiming" of Perry beside the Star City lynching of Clyde Ellison and the Birmingham killing of Sergt.-Major John Green. The editorial argued that such incidents shook "the very foundation of our loyalty" and called for legislation to secure fair treatment for Black citizens.

reader.title: Beating of Lieutenant Marion R. Perry
bases: A postal clerk struck Perry and then all the clerks in the store attacked him, wounding him with a shoe rack; no killing or threat to kill is reported (A5, A6).

The Chicago Defender and the Colorado Statesman print the same Little Rock dispatch word for word (A3, A5, A6), and the Statesman editorial (A4) adds no independent detail, so the story rests on one report.

accounts.label: Little Rock Black correspondent's dispatch
accounts.gist: Perry was refused a money order, asked why, was ordered to move away, and was struck by the clerk and then beaten by all the store's clerks, one wielding a shoe rack.

accounts.label: Colorado Statesman editorial
accounts.gist: Describes 'the terrible beating and maiming' of Perry after he asked a postoffice clerk why he was refused a money order, as one of a series of outrages in 1919.
